title: What compression codecs does Spark support — Snappy (fast, default, splittable), ZSTD (better ratio, modern), Gzip (good ratio, slower, not splittable), LZ4 (fast), Bzip2 (best ratio, slowest) — and at what levels can compression be applied (`spark.io.compression.codec`, shuffle, broadcast, checkpoint, event logs, RDD)?
shortTitle: What compression codecs does Spark support
topicTitle: What compression codecs does Spark support

s1_definition.profdef: Spark supports several compression codecs that trade off speed against compression ratio and splittability: Snappy is fast and splittable and is the default for Parquet output, ZSTD gives a better ratio with modern speed, Gzip gives a good ratio but is slow and not splittable, LZ4 is very fast with a modest ratio, and Bzip2 gives the best ratio but is the slowest and is splittable. Compression applies at two distinct layers: the output data format layer, controlled per writer, and the internal engine layer for shuffle, broadcast, checkpoint, event logs, and cached RDD blocks, controlled by `spark.io.compression.codec`.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India shipping boxes of documents between branches. A codec is how tightly you pack each box. Snappy packs quickly and the boxes can be opened by many workers at once, so it is the everyday default. Bzip2 packs the tightest so you pay the least for shipping, but packing and unpacking is painfully slow. Gzip packs well but each box must be opened by a single worker from the start because it cannot be split, so twenty workers cannot share one box. ZSTD is the modern choice that packs tight and still fast. There are two separate places this packing happens: the archives you store long term (the output files), and the temporary boxes Spark shuffles between its own workers internally.
s1_definition.oneliner: Choose Snappy or ZSTD for a good speed-and-ratio balance and splittability, avoid Gzip for large splittable reads, and remember output-format compression and internal `spark.io.compression.codec` are two separate settings.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark supports several compression codecs that trade off speed against compression ratio and splittability: Snappy is fast and splittable and is the default for Parquet output, ZSTD gives a better ratio with modern speed, Gzip gives a good ratio but is slow and not splittable, LZ4 is very fast with a modest ratio, and Bzip2 gives the best ratio but is the slowest and is splittable. Compression applies at two distinct layers: the output data format layer, controlled per writer, and the internal engine layer for shuffle, broadcast, checkpoint, event logs, and cached RDD blocks, controlled by `spark.io.compression.codec`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India shipping boxes of documents between branches. A codec is how tightly you pack each box. Snappy packs quickly and the boxes can be opened by many workers at once, so it is the everyday default. Bzip2 packs the tightest so you pay the least for shipping, but packing and unpacking is painfully slow. Gzip packs well but each box must be opened by a single worker from the start because it cannot be split, so twenty workers cannot share one box. ZSTD is the modern choice that packs tight and still fast. There are two separate places this packing happens: the archives you store long term (the output files), and the temporary boxes Spark shuffles between its own workers internally.

**One line to remember:** Choose Snappy or ZSTD for a good speed-and-ratio balance and splittability, avoid Gzip for large splittable reads, and remember output-format compression and internal `spark.io.compression.codec` are two separate settings.

sections.s2_technical:
Compression in Spark reduces the bytes written to storage and moved over the network, which lowers disk cost and input-output time, at the price of CPU to compress and decompress. The right codec depends on what you optimize for. Snappy is the default for Parquet because it decompresses very fast and its blocks are splittable, meaning a large file can be read by many tasks in parallel. ZSTD, enabled with `.option("compression", "zstd")`, typically achieves a noticeably smaller file than Snappy with competitive speed and is increasingly the recommended default for cold data. Gzip gives a good ratio but is slow and, critically, a single Gzip-compressed text file is not splittable, so one task must read the whole file from the start, which destroys parallelism on large files; it is fine inside Parquet because Parquet splits at the row-group level regardless. LZ4 is extremely fast with a modest ratio, good for hot shuffle data. Bzip2 gives the best ratio and is splittable for text, but it is so slow that it is rarely used except for archival.

You set output compression per writer, for example `df.write.option("compression", "zstd").parquet(path)`, or for text and JSON `.option("compression", "gzip")`. For ORC the option is the same, and for Avro you use the `avro.codec` option or the Spark option. The default compression for Parquet is Snappy, for ORC it is zlib or Snappy depending on version, and you should set it explicitly in production so it does not change under you.

Separately, the internal engine compresses its own temporary data. The property `spark.io.compression.codec`, which can be `lz4` (the default on modern Spark), `snappy`, `zstd`, or `lzf`, controls compression of shuffle output written between stages, broadcast variables sent to executors, RDD partitions cached with a serialized storage level, checkpoint data, and the event logs the history server reads. For example setting `spark.io.compression.codec=zstd` and `spark.shuffle.compress=true` compresses the shuffle files, which helps when the network is the bottleneck. There are fine-grained toggles too, such as `spark.shuffle.compress`, `spark.broadcast.compress`, `spark.rdd.compress`, and `spark.checkpoint.compress`, each of which turns compression on or off for that specific layer while using the codec from `spark.io.compression.codec`.

A senior-level nuance is that splittability matters enormously for reads: a single huge Gzip CSV cannot be parallelized, so many teams store raw data as Snappy or ZSTD Parquet precisely to keep it splittable and column-pruned. Another nuance is that compressing shuffle data is almost always a win because shuffle is network and disk bound, while over-compressing hot cached data with a slow codec can waste CPU; LZ4 is the sensible default for internal paths because it prioritizes speed. Finally, ZSTD supports a tunable level, so you can trade more CPU for a smaller file when storage cost dominates, which is useful for archival banking data retained for years.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the data lake stores years of settled trades. The team first wrote them as large Gzip-compressed CSV files because Gzip gave a nice small size. Months later, when analysts ran big scans, the jobs were painfully slow and used almost no parallelism, because each Gzip CSV file could only be read by a single task from the beginning. This is exactly the splittability problem: Gzip compresses well but a single Gzip text file is not splittable, so a cluster of a hundred cores reads one file with one core.

This is exactly how codec choice affects reads. Snappy and ZSTD Parquet files are splittable at the row-group level, so many tasks read one file in parallel, while a monolithic Gzip CSV serializes the read.

Problem 2 — The nightly pipeline also shuffles huge intermediate datasets between stages, and the network was the bottleneck. Turning on shuffle compression with a fast internal codec reduced the bytes crossing the network and sped up the stage boundaries. This is the separate internal-compression layer controlled by the engine's own codec setting, distinct from the output file format.

Because a real cluster is heavy, this runnable demo simulates codecs with representative speed and ratio profiles so the trade-offs are concrete and measurable. A `Codec` enum carries a relative speed factor, a compression ratio, and a splittable flag. A `CompressionProfiler` estimates compressed size and compress-plus-decompress time for a given raw size. A `ReadParallelismPlanner` shows how many tasks can read a file based on splittability. A `ShuffleLayer` applies the internal codec to simulated shuffle bytes. The demo compares the five codecs on a sample trade dataset for both output storage and shuffle, printing size, time, and achievable read parallelism so the right choice is obvious for each situation.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
spark:
  sql:
    parquet:
      compression:
        codec: zstd          # output format compression (zstd for cold data)
  io:
    compression:
      codec: lz4             # internal: shuffle/broadcast/rdd/checkpoint/event-log
  shuffle:
    compress: true
  broadcast:
    compress: true
  rdd:
    compress: true
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: ten gigabytes of raw settled-trade data to store, and four gigabytes of intermediate shuffle data moving between stages.

Step 1: The profiler estimates each codec on the ten gigabytes. Snappy produces about forty-five percent of the raw size quickly, ZSTD about thirty percent at slightly less speed, Gzip about thirty-three percent but much slower, LZ4 about fifty percent very fast, and Bzip2 about twenty-five percent but extremely slow. Each line reports the estimated size, round-trip time, and whether the format is splittable.

Step 2: The read planner takes each compressed size and computes how many tasks can read it. For the splittable codecs it divides the file size by the hundred-twenty-eight-megabyte split size to get many parallel tasks. For Gzip it returns one task and logs a warning, because a single Gzip text file cannot be split.

Step 3: The demo contrasts the real mistake. The Gzip CSV is modestly smaller on disk but can only be read by one task, so a large cluster is wasted. The ZSTD file is even smaller and is splittable, so the same data is read by many tasks in parallel.

Step 4: For the internal shuffle layer, the engine applies the fast LZ4 codec to the four gigabytes of shuffle data, compressing it to about half before it crosses the network, which reduces network time at the stage boundary.

Step 5: The demo then turns shuffle compression off and shows the full four gigabytes crossing the network, which on a network-bound stage is clearly worse, confirming that shuffle compression is almost always a win.

```
  ┌──────────────┐
  │   Codec       │ «enum»  SNAPPY/ZSTD/GZIP/LZ4/BZIP2
  │  + speed      │

  │  + splittable │
  └──────┬────────┘

   ▼     ▼                  ▼                   ▼
  CompressionProfiler  ReadParallelismPlanner  ShuffleLayer
  + compressedBytes()  + readTasks()           + networkBytes()
  + roundTripSeconds()

  Contract for readTasks:
    Pre:  file size in bytes + codec
    Post: splittable → ceil(size/128MB) tasks; not splittable → 1 task
    Rule: single huge Gzip text = 1 task = no parallelism

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. for each Codec: CompressionProfiler.profile(10GB)
  2. ReadParallelismPlanner.readTasks(size, codec)
  3. GZIP → 1 task (warn), ZSTD → 24 tasks (good)
  4. ShuffleLayer(LZ4,true).networkBytes(4GB) → 2GB
  5. ShuffleLayer(LZ4,false).networkBytes(4GB) → 4GB (warn)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark supports several compression codecs, and the choice is a trade-off between speed, compression ratio, and splittability. Snappy is fast and splittable and is the default for Parquet, ZSTD is the modern choice that gives a better ratio at competitive speed, Gzip gives a good ratio but is slow and, importantly, a single Gzip text file is not splittable, LZ4 is the fastest with a modest ratio, and Bzip2 gives the best ratio but is so slow it is really only for archival. Splittability is the detail that bites people, because a single large Gzip CSV can only be read by one task from the start, which throws away all the parallelism of a big cluster, whereas Snappy or ZSTD Parquet files split at the row-group level so many tasks read one file at once.

The second thing I always clarify is that there are two separate compression layers. The output-format compression is set per writer, for example writing Parquet with ZSTD for cold data or Snappy for hot data. Completely separate from that is the internal engine compression controlled by the io compression codec property, which compresses shuffle files between stages, broadcast variables, cached RDD blocks under serialized storage levels, checkpoint data, and the event logs. That internal codec defaults to LZ4 on modern Spark because the internal paths care most about speed, and there are individual toggles like shuffle compress, broadcast compress, and rdd compress that turn each layer on or off using that codec.

At the National Bank of India this came up twice. We first stored years of settled trades as large Gzip CSV files because Gzip looked small, and later big analytical scans were slow and barely parallel because each Gzip file was read by a single task. Switching the lake to ZSTD Parquet made the files even smaller and fully splittable, so scans used the whole cluster. Separately, a nightly pipeline was network bound at its shuffle stages, and turning on shuffle compression with the fast internal LZ4 codec cut the bytes crossing the network and sped up the stage boundaries. So my rule is to use Snappy or ZSTD Parquet for storage to keep reads parallel, reach for ZSTD at a higher level only when long-term storage cost dominates, and keep the internal codec on a fast option like LZ4 for shuffle and broadcast.
